sentences.text: Iris did not sleep well that night.
She kept the compass on her pillow, and every time she woke up, the needle was still pointing at the ceiling.
At breakfast, she showed her grandmother.
Grandmother Rose put down her toast.
She picked up the compass.
She held it flat.
She held it upside down.
She held it out the window, and up to the sky, and turned in a slow circle in the kitchen.
Then she put the compass on the table and sat down very hard.
"Iris," she said, "where did you find this?"
Iris told her.
About the butterflies.
About the map.
About the digging under the rose bush.
Her grandmother listened without interrupting.
When Iris had finished, Grandmother Rose was quiet for a long time.
"Come with me," she said.
"There's something in the study I need to show you."
The study was small and dark and full of old books and old papers and jars of dried leaves.
Grandmother Rose opened the bottom drawer of a wooden desk and pulled out a large leather-bound notebook.
The notebook was old.
The pages were yellow.
On the first page, in careful, spidery handwriting, was a name: ELEANOR HARWOOD, 1912.
"My grandmother," said Grandmother Rose.
"Your great-great-grandmother.
She kept butterflies too.
She kept them in a greenhouse in this same garden, and she noticed things nobody else noticed."
She turned the pages.
Sketches of butterflies.
Notes about wing patterns.
And, in the middle of the notebook, a drawing of a compass that looked exactly like the one on the kitchen table.
Iris read the note under the compass drawing.
It said: The butterflies do not fly to the North Star.
They fly to a red star, low in the east.
I have written to Professor Grant in London.
He does not believe me.
He says butterflies cannot navigate by any single star, and certainly not by a star as faint as that.
But I have watched them for four seasons and I am sure.
The star has no name that I know.
I will keep watching, and I will keep this compass safe for whoever comes after me.
The signature was ELEANOR HARWOOD, and the date was July, 1919.
"The star," said Grandmother Rose slowly, "is called Aldebaran.
It has a name now.
Scientists have known about it for a long time.
But last year — just last year, Iris — a research team in Norway announced that they had discovered something odd.
Aldebaran has a very unusual magnetic field.
They think some migratory insects might use it to navigate.
There was a paper about it in a journal I read."
She looked up at Iris.
"They are going to publish more research next year.
It will be a big discovery.
Nobody has ever proved it before."
She looked down at the notebook.
"My grandmother knew this," she said quietly.
"A hundred and six years before the scientists."
"And nobody believed her."
"Nobody believed her."
Iris looked at the compass.
She looked at the notebook.
She looked at her grandmother, who was smiling in a way that was mostly happy but a little bit sad.
"What do we do?" she asked.
Grandmother Rose thought for a moment.
"We write a letter," she said.
"To the research team in Norway.
We tell them what my grandmother wrote.
We send them a copy of the notebook.
Her name goes into the paper next to theirs.
A hundred years late, but it goes in."
Iris nodded.
"And Iris," said Grandmother Rose.
"Your name goes in too.
Because you're the one who found her."
That summer, Iris helped her grandmother write the letter.
It took them three weeks to get every sentence right.
The response came in the autumn.
It was signed by a Norwegian professor whose name Iris could not pronounce, and it said, in careful English:
Thank you.
We will publish.
Your great-great-grandmother was right, and we should have listened sooner.
Some knowledge waits a very long time for the right ears.
